summary: DCTCP is a TCP congestion control scheme for data centers. It builds on ECN by estimating what fraction of traffic sees congestion, and then shrinks the sending window in proportion. This keeps queues short and delay low. This informational RFC documents it rather than making it a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of slamming the brakes at the first sign of a traffic jam, it eases off in proportion to how crowded the road is.

questions: tcp congestion control for data centers
how does dctcp differ from standard tcp congestion control
subtitle: TCP congestion control that responds to congestion proportionally in data centers.

tldr.problem: Standard TCP detects congestion only by packet loss, which causes late reactions and unfair competition with ECN-aware endpoints in data centers with shallow buffers and bursty traffic patterns.
tldr.mechanism: DCTCP uses the Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) mechanism to estimate what fraction of traffic encountered congestion, then reduces the congestion window proportionally to that fraction rather than drastically cutting it in half.
tldr.outcome: This achieves higher throughput and lower latency with shallow-buffered switches in data centers. It is documented as an Informational RFC because it requires further standards work and must be deployed only in controlled intra-data-center environments.

today: RFC 8257 documents DCTCP as it is implemented in several major operating systems. It remains Informational because the IETF TCPM Working Group determined that a full standards specification would require additional work. DCTCP deployments continue in data center environments where the network is under single administrative control and both endpoints can be configured to use it.

sections.title: Why Data Centers Need Different Congestion Control
sections.content:
Data center networks have unique challenges: they use low-cost switches with small buffers, carry a mix of short and long flows at the same time, and experience sudden bursts where many servers send to one server simultaneously (called incast). Standard TCP, which detects congestion only when packets are dropped, reacts too slowly to these patterns. By the time TCP realizes there is congestion, queue delays have already grown and bursty traffic has mostly been dropped.

ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification) allows switches to mark packets instead of dropping them, but traditional ECN processing treats any mark as a sign to halve the congestion window, which is too drastic for mild congestion and causes long flows to lose throughput unnecessarily.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a school bus and a bicycle trying to share one narrow road. When they meet, the bicycle swerves hard and loses speed even if there is still room. DCTCP would let both adjust smoothly so they both keep moving.

sections.title: The Three-Part DCTCP Algorithm
sections.content: DCTCP changes how TCP uses ECN by involving three components working together. Layer 3 switches detect queue buildup and set the Congestion Encountered (CE) codepoint in the IP header when the queue exceeds a threshold. The receiver tracks the CE markings in arriving packets and echoes them back via the ECN-Echo (ECE) flag in TCP acknowledgments. The sender tracks what fraction of bytes it sent encountered congestion, then reduces its sending window not by a fixed amount but proportionally: if 10% of bytes saw congestion, it shrinks the window by a smaller amount than if 50% did.
sections.plainLanguage: A traffic light that changes from green to yellow tells drivers to slow down. DCTCP is like a dimmer: the brighter the light, the more drivers ease off the throttle, all at the same time.

sections.title: Estimating and Reacting to Congestion
sections.content:
DCTCP introduces a state variable, DCTCP.Alpha, that smooths the congestion estimate over time. Each round-trip time (RTT), the sender counts two things: how many bytes were acknowledged, and how many of those bytes carried the CE mark in ECN. The ratio M = bytes marked / bytes acked gives the current congestion level. DCTCP.Alpha is updated as DCTCP.Alpha = DCTCP.Alpha * (1 - g) + g * M, where g is the estimation gain (typically 1/16). The congestion window is then reduced by cwnd = cwnd * (1 - DCTCP.Alpha / 2), so mild congestion (low M) causes gentle reduction while severe congestion causes larger cuts.

The receiver implementation must also be aware of CE marks: it uses a state variable DCTCP.CE to send immediate acknowledgments when the congestion state changes, allowing the sender to track the congestion signal accurately even with delayed ACKs.
sections.plainLanguage: Every few seconds, count how many bumps happened in the road versus how many smooth stretches. If 1 in 10 was bumpy, easing off a little bit helps. If 5 in 10 were bumpy, ease off more.

sections.title: Deployment Challenges and Limitations
sections.content:
DCTCP must be deployed only within a data center under a single administrative domain. The RFC warns against deployment over the public Internet because DCTCP and standard TCP do not coexist well when both use the same congestion threshold: standard TCP will suffer packet loss and drastically cut its window, while DCTCP eases off gradually, causing DCTCP to seize a larger share of capacity. The entire network infrastructure must support ECN marking on switches and both endpoints must support DCTCP. Because DCTCP provides no negotiation mechanism, both sender and receiver must be configured out-of-band to use it together.

Implementations in Microsoft Windows Server 2012, Linux, and FreeBSD all follow this specification. Real-world deployments use DSCP (Differentiated Services Codepoint) to segregate DCTCP traffic from conventional TCP so they do not compete.
sections.plainLanguage: DCTCP only works when everybody in the network plays by the same rules. If a stranger with a different car joins the road, things break down.

sections.title: Security and Trade-offs
sections.content:
DCTCP inherits the security model of ECN: endpoints or the network can falsely report congestion to cause a sender to reduce its window, but this is no worse than simply dropping packets. The RFC notes one difference from ECN standards: setting the ECT (ECN-Capable Transport) codepoint on SYN and SYN-ACK packets poses security concerns on the open Internet but may be acceptable in controlled data centers, so DCTCP senders SHOULD set ECT on these control packets.

Known issues include inaccuracy when ACK packets are dropped, RTT unfairness (long-RTT flows are disadvantaged, as with all TCP), and lack of negotiation, which means misconfigured mixed deployments could behave unexpectedly. The RFC is Informational rather than Standards Track precisely because further experimental work is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could tell the road sensors there is congestion when there is not, but that is no worse than blocking the road. The real catch is that it only works when everyone agrees to use it.
